explanations.answer: Inquire of the LORD for them
explanations.explanation: Zedekiah, king of Judah, sends Pashhur and the priest Zephaniah to Jeremiah, the prophet. Their words are, “Please inquire of the LORD on our behalf, since Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is waging war against us.” Nebuchadnezzar is the king of Babylon, and his army is the reason for the visit. I think a city with an army at its door gets very interested in what a prophet has to say.

explanations.answer: Make peace with Babylon for them
explanations.explanation: Close, because the war is the whole reason for the visit. But the men don't ask Jeremiah to talk to Babylon. They say, “Please inquire of the LORD on our behalf…” Nobody here is handing him a tiny briefcase and sending him to the negotiating table.

explanations.answer: Lead the army out for them
explanations.explanation: The men don't ask Jeremiah to lead anything. What they ask is, “Please inquire of the LORD on our behalf…” Picture me leading an army, friend. I'd show up with a stamp, a mustache and a very confused look.

They say, “Perhaps the LORD will perform for us something like all His past wonders, so that Nebuchadnezzar will withdraw from us.” That word “Perhaps” tells you they're hoping. They want the LORD to act the way He has before. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is the one they want to see pack up and leave.

The text says the opposite. The men tell Jeremiah, “Perhaps the LORD will perform for us something like all His past wonders, so that Nebuchadnezzar will withdraw from us.” So they are hoping for a wonder. Nebuchadnezzar is the king of Babylon, and he's the one they want to see withdraw.

explanations.answer: The weapons in their own hands
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “I will turn against you the weapons of war in your hands…” Those weapons are what Zedekiah's people are using against the Chaldeans, Babylon's people, who besiege the city from outside the wall. The very weapons they are holding are the ones the LORD says He will turn against them. He names the weapons, and He doesn't name anything else here.

explanations.answer: The walls of their own city
explanations.explanation: The wall is mentioned, but only as the place the Chaldeans besiege the city from outside. The LORD says, “I will turn against you the weapons of war in your hands…” So it's the weapons they're holding, not the stones around them.

explanations.answer: The horses in their own stables
explanations.explanation: No horses show up in this verse. The LORD says, “I will turn against you the weapons of war in your hands…” These are the weapons Zedekiah's people are using to fight the Chaldeans, Babylon's people, who besiege the city from outside the wall. The stable stays quiet in this one.

The LORD says this to Zedekiah's people, and it's the other way around. He says, “And I Myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a mighty arm, with anger, fury, and great wrath.” So He is fighting against them, not for them. That's a heavy thing to read, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.

The LORD says, “And I Myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a mighty arm, with anger, fury, and great wrath.” He isn't fighting for Zedekiah's side. He is fighting against them. Zedekiah's men were hoping for a wonder like the ones in the past, and this isn't the kind they hoped for. This is a heavy part, friend.

The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar “…will put them to the sword; he will not spare them or show pity or compassion.” The ones handed over are Zedekiah, his officers and the people who survive the plague and sword and famine. This is a heavy verse, friend. I think this one hurts.

explanations.answer: He will make them his servants
explanations.explanation: That isn't what the verse says. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar “…will put them to the sword; he will not spare them or show pity or compassion.” Nothing in these words has them working for him. It's a heavy verse, and it's best to take it as it's written.

explanations.answer: He will send them home to Judah
explanations.explanation: That isn't what the verse says. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar “…will put them to the sword; he will not spare them or show pity or compassion.” There's no trip home in these words. This is a heavy verse, friend.

The LORD says, “…whoever goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who besiege you will live; he will retain his life like a spoil of war.” That's a strange path, because going out looks like giving up. But it's the way of life the LORD set before them in verse 8. Staying in the city is the other way.

The LORD says the opposite: “Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine and plague…” Staying is the way of death in these verses. The one who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans is the one who will live. It's the hard way to hear it, friend, but that's what's written.

A palace is a fine hiding spot, but it's still inside the city. The LORD says, “Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine and plague…” The ones who live are those who go out and surrender to the Chaldeans. A nice room doesn't change which side of the wall you're on.

The LORD says the city “…will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, who will destroy it with fire.” Fire turns up again in this passage when the LORD speaks to the house of David. I know fire from my ovens, friend, and this isn't the cozy kind. This is a serious word.
No water in this verse. The LORD says the king of Babylon “…will destroy it with fire.” Fire is the word, and it comes back later when the LORD speaks to the house of David.

An earthquake isn't mentioned here. The verse says the city will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, “…who will destroy it with fire.” The destroyer is the king of Babylon, and the tool is fire.

The LORD says, “Administer justice every morning, and rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor…” He speaks it to the house of David, the royal family. It's a daily job, not a once in a while one. I think a person who's rescued from an oppressor would be glad it was every morning.

Offerings aren't what's named here. The LORD says, “Administer justice every morning, and rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor…” The job is justice, and it goes with rescuing someone who has been robbed. The house of David is the family hearing it.

Taxes would make for a very grumpy morning, friend. But the LORD tells the house of David, “Administer justice every morning, and rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor…” The word is justice. The royal family is the one being addressed.

The LORD says, “…or My wrath will go forth like fire and burn with no one to extinguish it because of their evil deeds.” That's the other side of the daily job of justice. The house of David is the one being warned.

The text says it plainly. The LORD tells the house of David that if they don't do this, “…My wrath will go forth like fire and burn with no one to extinguish it because of their evil deeds.” So this is a real warning, and it's tied to the daily work of justice.

explanations.answer: No one can come against us
explanations.explanation: They say, “Who can come against us? Who can enter our dwellings?” I think that's the talk of people who feel safe up on their rocky plateau. I bet a great view can make a person feel pretty tall. But the LORD says, “Behold, I am against you…”

explanations.answer: The LORD will always protect us
explanations.explanation: That line isn't in the verse. What the LORD quotes them saying is, “Who can come against us? Who can enter our dwellings?” They are talking about no one coming against them. And the LORD says He Himself is against them.

explanations.answer: Egypt will come to save us
explanations.explanation: Egypt, a neighboring nation, doesn't come up in this verse. The people say, “Who can come against us? Who can enter our dwellings?” They are sure that no one can reach them. Then the LORD says, “Behold, I am against you…”

explanations.answer: Foreigners and the fatherless and widows
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “Do no wrong or violence to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow.” He says it right after telling the king to rescue the victim of robbery. These are people who might not have much to stand on, and the LORD names them one by one. I think that tells us they matter to Him.

Not this time. The LORD says, “Do no wrong or violence to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow.” Priests, prophets and scribes aren't in the list. The three named are the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow.

None of those are named in this verse. The LORD tells the king, “Do no wrong or violence to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow.” Those are the three. The message is for the king, his officials and his people who enter these gates.

The LORD says that if they carry out these commands, “…kings who sit on David’s throne will enter through the gates of this palace riding on chariots and horses…” It's a good picture, with kings coming in with their officials and their people. This is the bright side of the big IF. It all hangs on carrying out the commands.

The text says it's true. The LORD says that if they will indeed carry out these commands, “…kings who sit on David’s throne will enter through the gates of this palace riding on chariots and horses…” They would come with their officials and their people. It's the good side of the IF.

The LORD says, “…I swear by Myself, declares the LORD, that this house will become a pile of rubble.” He swears by Himself, which is as serious as it gets. This is the other side of the IF. The word is for the king, his officials and his people.
There's no prison in this verse. The LORD says, “…I swear by Myself, declares the LORD, that this house will become a pile of rubble.” So the word is rubble. And He swears by Himself.

That's not what the LORD swears here. He says, “…I swear by Myself, declares the LORD, that this house will become a pile of rubble.” Babylon's king isn't named in that oath, friend. The word is rubble.

The text says the opposite. The LORD says, “…I will surely turn you into a desert, like cities that are uninhabited.” He says “surely,” so this is a firm word. He first says the house is like Gilead and like the summit of Lebanon. Then comes the turn.

The LORD says, “…I will surely turn you into a desert, like cities that are uninhabited.” He says “surely,” so there's no maybe in it. Right before this He calls the house like Gilead and like the summit of Lebanon. It's a big drop from there to a desert, friend.

The LORD says the destroyers “…will cut down the choicest of your cedars and throw them into the fire.” These destroyers come, each man with his weapons. Cedars are tall trees, and the choicest ones are named. A timber pile has never looked so sad.

Vineyards aren't in this verse. The LORD says the destroyers “…will cut down the choicest of your cedars and throw them into the fire.” Cedars are the trees named, and the choicest ones are singled out.

Fig trees aren't mentioned here. The LORD says the destroyers “…will cut down the choicest of your cedars and throw them into the fire.” Cedars are the trees named. The destroyers come with their weapons, and the choicest ones go.

explanations.answer: They forsook the LORD's covenant and served other gods
explanations.explanation: People will reply, “Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and have worshiped and served other gods.” Many nations pass by and ask why, and this is the answer given. It's the reason in the text, plain and simple. A covenant is a promise the LORD made with His people, and they turned from it.

explanations.answer: They ignored the LORD's prophets and trusted in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Those details aren't in this verse. The answer people give is, “Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and have worshiped and served other gods.” Egypt, a neighboring nation, isn't mentioned in that answer. The reason is about the covenant and other gods.

explanations.answer: They neglected the LORD's temple and stopped His offerings
explanations.explanation: The temple and offerings aren't named in the answer. People reply, “Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and have worshiped and served other gods.” That's the reason the verse gives. It's about the covenant and other gods, friend.
